text: What does it mean to say an encoding is an agreement rather than a fact?
choices: That it could have been otherwise, that both parties must hold the same one, and that nothing in the data enforces it.
That encodings are arbitrary, so no encoding is better than any other.
That the agreement is written down in a standard, which is what makes it binding.
That encodings are conventions and therefore cannot be verified or tested.
explanation: All three clauses matter, and the first distractor is the misreading to guard against: agreements can be better or worse. Two's complement was chosen because it makes one adder do subtraction; UTF-8 was designed to be ASCII-compatible and self-synchronizing. Chapter 35 returns to this — the difference between a good agreement and a bad one is what becomes possible afterward.
